assumptions: A CSV-only historical spot-FX cost audit that excludes custody, execution, and hedging recommendations can be offered lawfully after scoped Polish legal review.
A reachable subset of Polish SMEs has recurring non-PLN conversion volume and avoidable all-in cost large enough to justify the proposed diagnostic fee.
Timestamped executable comparison quotes for the relevant currency pairs and transaction sizes can be licensed at a cost compatible with service margins.
Clients can agree in advance to a savings baseline that separates provider pricing from timing, liquidity, credit, settlement, transaction-size, and service differences.
The founder can pilot delivery within five hours per day using client exports and contractors without relying on confidential employer resources.
Accountants or fractional CFOs can refer qualified buyers on commercially acceptable, nonexclusive terms, although no commitment or acquisition performance is yet established.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Run paid pilots with a tightly specified high-volume Polish-SME segment and capture complete transaction coverage, buyer-approved contemporaneous executable benchmarks, realized net savings after switching costs, delivery and dispute hours, quote-data and compliance cost, channel CAC and conversion, and quarterly renewal. In parallel, obtain scoped Polish legal advice and signed data-provider and referral terms that establish permitted use, cost, and continuity.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: FX costs can be opaque across bank, card, and payment routes, and transaction-cost analysis can turn a diffuse finance expense into an auditable procurement problem. The independent, no-execution stance reduces seller conflict, but the mechanism is established rather than novel and depends on difficult benchmark selection and data access.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A named large-company engagement and the existence of formal FX-cost reviews support real economic pain, especially for firms with substantial recurring conversions. However, no evidence establishes that Polish SMEs will pay the proposed upfront fee plus savings share, and low-cost providers or free incumbent audits may solve simpler cases cheaply.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: An upfront diagnostic can fund acquisition and initial work, while a success fee aligns incentives and creates attractive cash conversion if savings are unambiguous. The central economics remain unresolved: recoverable leakage, accepted counterfactuals, analyst hours, quote-data cost, compliance and insurance overhead, disputes, retention, and the proposed 55-75% contribution margin are all unverified; the 800-client wealth path is illustrative rather than supported.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish trade flows create a substantial top-down context, and importers with recurring non-PLN payments are identifiable in principle. Yet the target is not narrowed by currency mix, converted volume, incumbent markup, transaction complexity, or reachable savings, and SME counts overstate the economically relevant high-volume subset.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Independence and transparent attribution could earn trust in a focused niche, but the company would not control client records, execution, or the provider decision. Moneycorp can offer free audits through partners, Revolut can remove straightforward leakage with transparent pricing, and Kantox or similar platforms can absorb analysis into a broader treasury workflow, leaving little demonstrated basis for segment domination.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful audit wedge could extend into recurring monitoring, provider tenders, policy controls, exposure analytics, and additional CEE markets. Those adjacencies are commercially coherent, but several move toward regulated data access, hedging, or integrated treasury capabilities already offered by stronger incumbents.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Lawfully retained cross-client execution observations could eventually improve benchmarks, but permission to reuse them is unproven and meaningful FX analysis also requires comparable market data. Client access is nonexclusive, revocable, and replaceable, while generic ingestion and reconciliation logic is readily replicable; no durable data, contractual, workflow, or distribution moat exists in v1.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A vendor-neutral review can be more credible than an execution provider's sales-led audit, and outcome-linked pricing can reduce perceived buyer risk. The packet does not show a sufficiently large, consistent, or uniquely measurable improvement over free audits, direct switching to a transparent provider, or integrated treasury software to reliably change SME behavior.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Digital transaction records, provider choice, and regulatory disclosure make cost review more feasible, while large Polish trade flows sustain the underlying need. At the same time, mature fintech and treasury products already bundle pricing, execution, approval, and reporting, and greater disclosure reduces some of the information asymmetry the service targets.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Accountants and fractional CFOs are plausible trusted channels, and the fixed diagnostic could cover founder-led acquisition if conversion is adequate. There is no partner commitment, lead-volume, conversion, referral-cost, or CAC evidence, the arrangements are nonexclusive, and execution providers already court the same partners with free audits and supporting tools.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A bounded historical spot-FX audit using client exports is capital-light, technically aligned with the founder, and feasible to pilot part-time with AI-assisted normalization. Reliable delivery still requires licensed comparable quotes, sensitive-data controls, a defensible savings protocol, negotiation expertise, legal advice on recommendations and compensation, and either regulated partners or deliberately manual ingestion; scaling the service beyond the founder is materially harder than launching it.

highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the beachhead to firms above a validated annual FX-volume and complexity threshold, then replace the revocable one-off audit with an accountant- or ERP-embedded recurring FX procurement checkpoint backed by licensed executable quote data, a contractually agreed savings protocol, and subscription plus tender-outcome pricing; this would improve data continuity, retention, attribution, and channel control together.
main_structural_strength: A capital-light, conflict-reduced managed-service wedge can convert messy historical FX transactions into measurable procurement savings, aligns well with the founder's data and finance capabilities, and can charge partly on independently verified outcomes.
primary_score_limiter: There is no validated economic core for the target Polish-SME segment: willingness to pay, recoverable leakage, buyer-accepted attribution, fully loaded delivery cost, CAC, and repeat revenue are all unknown, while credible substitutes can subsidize or bundle the same diagnostic.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The proposed audit and referral wedge is already contestable from three directions: Moneycorp offers partners a free client FX audit, Revolut Business offers Polish firms low-cost exchange plus finance workflow features, and Kantox integrates data capture, execution, and reporting. Because client data access is nonexclusive and revocable, these substitutes can undercut the fee and retain the downstream relationship rather than merely copy a feature.
